  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Known People: Related people, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Ravi, a forty-nine-year-old military medic, had spent two decades tending to soldiers in field hospitals and clinic wards, but the damage he carried was not from any war zone. It came from the woman he had loved in his thirties, a relationship that ended one night when she turned on him with a fury he still could not explain. She had been drinking; he remembered the sour smell of sweat and alcohol as she pinned him to the floor, her knee in his ribs, her fists coming down on his chest and arms. He was trained to immobilise a combatant, but he did not fight back. He could not. He was certain that if he hurt her, he would be the one blamed. When he finally called the police, they arrived quickly—two officers in crisp uniforms—but after taking statements, they told him it was a “domestic dispute” and left without pressing charges. She faced no consequences. Ravi was left with the memory, and with a quiet, corrosive certainty that something in him must have deserved it.

In the months and years that followed, Ravi’s life narrowed. He stopped wearing the style of shirt he had worn that night—a plain grey crewneck—because the sight of it in his closet brought the scene back as if it were happening now. He could not put the event into words; when his current wife, Anjali, asked what had happened with his ex, he could only shake his head. The sensations were what returned: the sharp pain in his ribs when he remembered, the feeling of being pinned, the smell of sweat. That odour haunted him most. He began avoiding the gym entirely, even though he had always been physically active, because the smell of his own perspiration or another person’s triggered a visceral reliving that left him drenched in cold sweat and shaking. At work, he started to avoid colleagues and patients alike, taking administrative duties that kept him in a back office. He only felt safe in a very limited number of places—his bedroom at home with the door locked, and one supply closet at the hospital where no one ever came. Ordinary sounds, like the click of a door latch or the hum of a fluorescent light, made him jump as if a threat were upon him.

Sleep became a problem because Ravi felt he had to stay alert. He lay awake for hours, scanning for movement, listening for footsteps, his body tense. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that he was defective, marked by what had happened. Nothing felt meaningful anymore; his work, once a source of pride as he saved lives, seemed hollow. The people who had hurt him—his ex-partner and the system that let her walk free—had faced no accountability, and that injustice gnawed at him more than he admitted.

He only sought help when his avoidance began to fracture his marriage. Anjali had started to cry during an argument, telling him she felt like a stranger. That night, lying in their bed with his back to her, Ravi realised he could not remember the last time he had let himself be fully present. What frightened him most was the thought that he was beyond repair—that the defect he felt was not a wound but a truth about who he was. Still, he made the appointment, and in the therapist’s office, he sat with his hands clenched, hoping that maybe, if he could find a way to speak the unspeakable, something might finally shift.

The vignette does not describe any current trigger from related people; only general avoidance of people is mentioned, not specific to known individuals.
